kits.familyName: Putting a process idea to work
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you to find a faster way to handle {task|the}, and you have an idea.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you were asked by {lead|the} to speed up {task|the}. You have come up with a new method.
pressure: {coworker3} says you should just start the new method today and sort out details later.
detail: The idea came to you while restocking the {area}.
You sketched the idea on a notepad during lunch.

tiers.1: A required quality check protects people, so it comes before speed.
tiers.2: Knowing why the last attempt failed shapes everything else about the idea.
tiers.3: The people whose work changes need a say before the change happens.
tiers.4: A purchase request is stronger once the idea itself is settled.

fact: Your new method skips a quality check that {lead|the} requires on every {deliverable}.
clear: {Lead|the} looked over your method and confirmed it keeps every required check.
issues.done: the method was already confirmed to keep the required checks
issues.action: Rework the method so the required quality check stays in place.
issues.brief: rework the method to keep the quality check
issues.reason: A faster process that drops a required check trades reliability for speed. Keeping the check protects the people who depend on the work.
issues.lesson: Improve a process without removing the steps that protect quality and safety.

shortcut.text: Try the faster method on today's work and see whether anything goes wrong.
shortcut.brief: try it on today's work and see
shortcut.why: Testing on real work without the required check puts that work, and the people relying on it, at risk.
shortcut.mis: The only way to know if a shortcut is safe is to try it on real work.

fact: {coworker} mentions that a similar change was tried last year and dropped, but nobody remembers why.
clear: {coworker} found the old notes: the earlier change was dropped only because a supplier closed.
issues.done: you already know why the earlier attempt was dropped
issues.action: Find out why the earlier attempt was dropped before going further with yours.
issues.brief: find out why the earlier attempt was dropped
issues.reason: Learning why the last attempt was dropped lets you fix that problem in your version instead of repeating it.
issues.lesson: Learn from earlier attempts before pushing a similar change.

shortcut.text: Drop your idea, since something similar already failed once.
shortcut.brief: drop the idea because it failed before
shortcut.why: A past failure may have had a fixable cause. Dropping the idea without knowing why may waste a good improvement.
shortcut.mis: If something failed once, it will always fail.

fact: The change would also alter how {coworker2} prepares work for you each morning.
clear: {coworker2} has already looked at your method and is glad to try it.
issues.done: {coworker2} has already agreed to the change
issues.action: Talk with {coworker2} about how the change would affect that morning work.
issues.reason: People whose work changes can spot problems you cannot, and they deserve a say before their routine changes.
issues.lesson: Involve the people a change affects before you put it in place.

shortcut.text: Start the new method and let {coworker2} adjust as needed.
shortcut.why: Changing someone's routine without talking to them causes confusion and misses their useful input.
shortcut.mis: People will adapt to a better process without being asked.

fact: The method needs a new storage rack, and purchases need approval from {lead|the}.
clear: {Lead|the} has already approved buying the new storage rack.
issues.action: Give {lead|the} a short note on the rack's cost and the time it saves.
issues.brief: give {lead|the} a note on cost and time saved
issues.reason: Purchases need approval, and a clear cost-and-benefit note helps the lead decide quickly.
issues.lesson: Back an idea that needs resources with a short case for its cost and benefit.

shortcut.text: Buy the rack yourself and ask to be paid back later.
shortcut.brief: buy the rack yourself and ask for repayment
shortcut.why: Purchases need approval first. Buying it yourself skips that decision and may not be repaid.
shortcut.mis: Paying for something yourself means you do not need approval.

proceed.text: Put the new method into use and track how much time it saves.
proceed.why: The lead asked for this improvement and nothing in the situation stands in the way. Tracking the time saved shows whether it works.
proceed.lesson: Once an idea has been checked, shared and cleared, put it to work and measure the result.

generic.text: Keep the idea to yourself until you are sure it is perfect.
generic.why: Waiting for a perfect idea delays the improvement the lead asked for. Ideas improve through sharing and testing.
generic.mis: An idea should be perfect before anyone hears it.

generic.text: Ask {lead|the} to come up with a different idea instead.
generic.why: The lead asked you for an idea. Handing the task back without working through the issues wastes your idea.
generic.mis: Problems with an idea mean someone else should solve it.

overcaution.text: Hold off until every coworker on every shift has reviewed the method.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation calls for more review, and waiting on everyone stalls an improvement that is ready.
overcaution.mis: More review always makes an idea safer.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and {lead|the} asked you to improve how {task|the} is done.

steps.text: Time how long the current process takes
Ask why the earlier change was dropped
Try the new method for one week
Compare the new times with the old ones

rel: You need the starting time to measure any improvement.
Fix the earlier problem before trying the method again.
Affected coworkers should agree before their routine changes.
The rack has to be approved before the method can run.
There is nothing to compare until the trial has run.
process.lesson: Measure first, clear the obstacles, test the idea, then compare results.

title: Proposal: a faster way to handle {task|the}
intro: You drafted this proposal for {lead|the}. Read it once more before sending.
doc.lesson: A strong proposal states the problem, the evidence and the cost, and keeps the safeguards.

lines.text: Right now, {task|the} takes about 40 minutes each day.
lines.fine: Stating the current situation with a measurement sets up the comparison.

lines.text: I suggest keeping the supplies for it together on one rack.
In a one-week trial at my station, it took about 25 minutes a day.
lines.fine: A small trial with measured results is good evidence.

bad.text: I have not tried it yet, but I am sure it will save at least an hour a day.
bad.why: The claim has no evidence behind it, and an hour is more than the whole task takes. Proposals should rest on measured results.

lines.text: The required quality check stays in place at the end.
lines.fine: The proposal keeps the safeguard that protects the work.

bad.text: To save time, we would stop doing the quality check at the end.
bad.why: Dropping a required check trades quality for speed. An improvement should keep the safeguards.

lines.text: The rack costs about $60, which I would like your approval to buy.
lines.fine: The cost is stated and approval is requested before buying.

bad.text: I already bought the rack with the store account, so it is ready to go.
bad.why: Purchases need approval first. Spending without it bypasses the person responsible for the budget.

lines.text: {coworker2}, whose morning work this changes, helped plan it and supports it.
lines.fine: The proposal shows the affected coworker was involved.

bad.text: {coworker2} will have to reorganize the morning prep, but I have not mentioned it yet.
bad.why: The change alters a coworker's routine without involving them. That person should be consulted before the proposal goes forward.

lines.text: Could we talk about it this week?
lines.fine: A clear, polite request for a next step.

review.notes: Approval requirement for purchases is stated in the scenario. Tiers: required check > learning from history > consulting affected people > purchase case.

setup: Your team at {workplace|the} is meeting to brainstorm ways to reduce crowding in the {area}.
You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, in a team meeting about how to make the {area} less crowded.
pressure: {coworker3} says the meeting has to end in five minutes.
{coworker3} keeps saying the team should just pick something.
detail: The meeting is being held in the break room.
Someone brought coffee for the group.

tiers.1: An idea that blocks an emergency exit cannot go forward in any form.
tiers.2: The stated budget limit decides which ideas are even possible.
tiers.3: Hearing every voice comes before choosing among ideas.
tiers.4: Comparing options leads to a better choice than taking the first one.
tiers.5: Giving credit matters, but it can wait until the ideas are settled.

fact: The most popular suggestion so far would put shelving in front of the emergency exit.
issues.action: Point out that the shelving would block the exit and suggest moving it elsewhere.
issues.brief: point out the blocked exit and suggest another spot
issues.reason: An emergency exit must stay clear. Raising the problem while suggesting an alternative keeps the idea alive without the danger.
issues.lesson: Creative ideas still have to keep people safe; adapt the idea rather than accept the risk.

shortcut.text: Go along with the shelving idea, since most of the team likes it.
shortcut.brief: go along with the popular shelving idea
shortcut.why: Popularity does not make a blocked exit safe. Someone needs to raise the problem now.
shortcut.mis: If most people like an idea, it must be fine.

fact: {Lead|the} has said the fix must use only furniture and supplies already on hand.
issues.action: Suggest ideas that rearrange or reuse what the team already has.
issues.brief: suggest ideas that reuse what you already have
issues.reason: The lead set a clear limit. Ideas that fit it can actually happen, and creativity with existing resources is still creativity.
issues.lesson: Work within stated limits; constraints are a prompt for creative reuse.

shortcut.text: Push for new shelving units, since buying them would work best.
shortcut.why: The lead ruled out new purchases. An idea that ignores the limit cannot be used.
shortcut.mis: The best idea is the one with the best result, whatever the limits.

fact: {coworker} works in the {area} every day but has not had a chance to speak.
clear: {coworker} has already shared an idea, and the group wrote it on the board.
issues.done: {coworker} has already had a turn to share
issues.action: Invite {coworker} to share ideas before the group moves on.
issues.reason: The person who works in the space daily may know what causes the crowding. Inviting that input makes the solution better.
issues.lesson: Draw out ideas from everyone, especially the people closest to the problem.

shortcut.text: Assume {coworker} would have spoken up if there were a good idea.
shortcut.why: People stay quiet for many reasons. Missing the daily user's view can mean missing the real fix.
shortcut.mis: Quiet people have nothing to contribute.

fact: The group is about to adopt the first idea mentioned without hearing any others.
clear: The group has already listed and compared five ideas on the board.
issues.done: the group already compared several ideas
issues.short: the rush to the first idea
issues.action: Suggest listing a few more ideas and comparing them before choosing.
issues.brief: suggest comparing a few more ideas
issues.reason: The first idea is rarely the best one. A few minutes of comparison often turns up a simpler or cheaper option.
issues.lesson: Generate several options and compare them before committing to one.

shortcut.text: Agree to the first idea so the meeting can end on time.
shortcut.brief: agree to the first idea to finish early
shortcut.why: Ending on time is nice, but choosing without comparing may lock in a weak solution.
shortcut.mis: The first workable idea is good enough.

fact: The idea you plan to share builds on a suggestion {coworker2} made last month.
issues.action: Share your idea and mention that it builds on {coworker2}'s earlier suggestion.
issues.reason: Naming where an idea came from is honest and encourages others to keep contributing.
issues.lesson: Give credit for the ideas you build on; it keeps people contributing.

shortcut.text: Present the idea as entirely your own to make a strong impression.
shortcut.brief: present the idea as entirely yours
shortcut.why: Taking credit for a coworker's thinking is unfair and discourages future ideas.
shortcut.mis: Getting noticed matters more than giving credit.

proceed.text: Help the group choose an idea and agree on who will try it first.
proceed.why: The ideas have been heard and compared, so the next useful step is a decision and a plan to act on it.
proceed.lesson: Once ideas are heard and compared, move the group to a decision and next steps.

generic.text: Stay quiet so the meeting does not get any longer.
generic.why: Holding back your input deprives the team of ideas and leaves problems unraised.
generic.mis: Speaking up only slows a meeting down.

generic.text: Criticize each idea as soon as it is suggested.
generic.why: Shooting down ideas immediately makes people stop sharing. Evaluation works better after ideas are collected.

overcaution.text: Suggest scheduling another meeting so everyone can think longer.
overcaution.why: The ideas are already heard and compared. Another meeting delays a decision the group is ready to make.
overcaution.mis: More time always produces better ideas.

setup: Your team at {workplace|the} is running a short brainstorm about crowding in the {area}.

steps.text: Agree on the problem the group is solving
Compare the ideas and choose one

rel: People need to know the problem before suggesting fixes.
Knowing the limits keeps ideas realistic.
The limit applies to a defined problem.
All ideas, including the quiet person's, come in before choosing.
The invitation comes once the problem is clear.
You can only compare ideas once they are collected.
process.lesson: Define the problem and the limits, gather ideas from everyone, then compare and choose.

title: Brainstorm notes: crowding in the {area}
intro: You took these notes at the team brainstorm. Check them before sharing with the group.
doc.lesson: Brainstorm notes should capture every idea fairly and record decisions that respect the limits.

lines.text: Goal: reduce crowding in the {area} during busy times.
lines.fine: A clear statement of the problem.

lines.text: Limit: use only furniture and supplies already on hand.
Ideas: stagger break times, move the supply cart, add a second entry lane.
lines.fine: Several options are recorded for comparison.

lines.text: Ideas came from all five people at the meeting.
lines.fine: The notes show every voice was included.

bad.text: Ideas came from the three most experienced people; the others did not need to add anything.
bad.why: Leaving out newer people's ideas wastes their view of the problem and discourages participation.

lines.text: Any change must keep the emergency exit clear.

bad.text: Decision: stack the extra boxes in front of the side exit door.
bad.why: Blocking an exit creates a serious danger in an emergency. No space-saving idea is worth that.

lines.text: Decision: stagger break times for two weeks, then review.
lines.fine: A decision with a trial period and review.

bad.text: Decision: order two new storage cabinets this week.
bad.why: The notes already say only items on hand may be used. Ordering cabinets breaks the stated limit.

lines.text: The staggered-break idea was first raised by {coworker2} last month.
lines.fine: Credit is given for the original idea.

bad.text: The staggered-break idea is credited only to the note taker.
bad.why: The idea came from a coworker. Notes should credit people fairly.

review.notes: Budget limit stated by the lead; exit-safety tier is general practice, stated without legal claims.
